papers.title: Manifesting inspired landscapes: Implementing a plural valuation framework for landscape restoration in South Africa
papers.authors: Ancois Carien de Villiers, Jessica J. Cockburn, Marja J. Spierenburg, Karen  Joan Esler
papers.abstract: Abstract Context Plural valuation frameworks integrate different values of sustainability and could help navigate the often messy and contentious nature of multistakeholder collaborations to restore multifunctional landscapes. However, several literature reviews have concluded that this potential has not yet been realised in practice. Objectives To understand this theory–practice gap, a realist case study was implemented to explore the experience of a non-profit company, Living Lands, in adapting Commonland’s 4Returns framework to the contested and complex context of two South African landscapes. The framework is intended to enable a long-term perspective on landscape restoration, and deepen understanding on how livelihoods are supported by ecological, economic, and social outcomes emergent from social-ecological relationships. Methods Interviews with and participant observations of Living Lands, landscape community members, and other stakeholders were used to assess the implementation and outcomes of projects based on the framework. Data analysis included thematic coding of transcripts, fieldnotes, and documents. Results The 4Returns framework enabled collective sensemaking, and broadened the value of restoration. However, participants highlighted pitfalls of oversimplified linear understandings of complex challenges, particularly in terms of securing financial returns, engaging marginalised people as fellow stewards, and the role of inspiration (i.e. visioning, learning, and innovations). Conclusions To manifest the potential of plural valuation frameworks, implementation requires an active and continuous reflexive process to support practitioners in engaging with social-ecological relationships. This includes recognising marginalised community members as stewards and not passive beneficiaries of projects, and managing expectations while maintaining inspiration to weather setbacks inherent to transformative processes for landscape sustainability.

papers.title: Development and application of a risk characterisation and categorisation approach for predicted road runoff concentrations
papers.authors: Lian Lundy, Mike Revitt, Bryan Ellis
papers.abstract: Road runoff is a key source of pollution entering receiving waters yet identifying where its discharge is prejudicial to water quality remains a challenge. Addressing this need is an emerging policy and practical issue, with the recast EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive requiring identification of locations where separately piped runoff poses a risk to the environment or public health. As a contribution, this study presents a novel approach for the risk characterisation and categorisation of road runoff outfalls based on the comparison of predicted environmental concentrations (PECs) with derived predicted no-effect concentrations (PNECs). Specifically, an established emissions-based approach was used to predict concentrations of total suspended solids, zinc, copper, lead and cadmium in road runoff discharging from 126 sections of road under three rainfall scenarios (i.e. PECs). The development of PNECs involved the translation of water quality threshold values into equivalent runoff concentrations through a stepwise process incorporating bioavailability and partitioning behaviour (as appropriate), and a range of receiving water dilution factors (from 2:1 to 50:1). This allowed the calculation of risk characterisation ratios, enabling road runoff outfalls to be allocated into risk categories. Results indicate that total suspended solids and zinc present the greatest risk across sites, with dilution factors of 50:1 insufficient to mitigate impacts for all road sections under all scenarios. The proposed approach provides a transparent, adaptable tool to support the identification and prioritisation of high-risk road runoff outfalls, offering an evidence base for targeting where to install mitigation measures within integrated urban water management planning.

papers.title: Quantifying the relationship between prescribed burning and wildfire severity in south-eastern Australia
papers.authors: Charlie Hart, Luke Collins, Tom A. Fairman et al.
papers.abstract: High-severity wildfires can pose a critical threat to society and forest ecosystems. While prescribed burning is widely applied to mitigate these risks, evaluation of its effectiveness at the landscape level remains challenging. Factors hindering these assessments include a lack of spatial data quantifying the amount of fuel treatment within burns, and challenges in controlling for variation in environmental conditions (e.g., weather, topography) that affect wildfire severity. We evaluated the effect of historical prescribed burns on wildfire severity in south-eastern Australia. We accounted for spatial variation in fuel treatments by objectively classifying the severity of ∼1300 prescribed burns conducted in the decade preceding each wildfire. Using a Random Forest modelling approach, we identified the key drivers of wildfire severity and employed counterfactual scenarios to quantify the landscape-scale influence of these prescribed burns while controlling the influence of environmental covariates. Overall, fire weather and aridity were the strongest drivers of wildfire severity. Recent prescribed burning reduced the extent of higher severity classes, relatively consistently across climatic conditions. Counterfactual scenarios showed that prescribed burning reduced the total area of the two highest wildfire severity classes (high canopy scorch and canopy burnt) by 6.2% (2882 ha) and nearly doubled the area that remained unburnt within treated areas. Our findings support the strategic use of prescribed burning to reduce the extent of high-severity fire. However, managers must remain mindful of the ecological trade-offs from increased frequency of low intensity prescribed fire, to ensure that fuel reduction prescriptions support forest resilience in an ever-warming climate.

papers.title: Life cycle assessment of marine biodiversity restoration: Case study of European flat oyster (Ostrea edulis) in Nora Lagoon
papers.authors: Erica Gagliano, Stefano Spotorno, Gianni Brundu et al.
papers.abstract: Marine ecosystem restoration is increasingly recognized as a key strategy to reverse biodiversity loss and support the recovery of ecosystem services. However, the environmental burdens generated by restoration activities are rarely quantified. This study investigates whether Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) can support the design and management of environmentally sustainable marine restoration interventions. Using the restoration of the European flat oyster ( Ostrea edulis ) in the Nora Lagoon (Italy) as a case study, a cradle-to-deployment LCA was performed, including adult collection, hatchery stage at laboratory scale, transportation, and field deployment. Environmental impacts were assessed and complemented by LCA-based biodiversity indicators, sensitivity analyses, and an evaluation of shell-based carbon sequestration potential. Results showed that the deployment phase was the main contributor to global warming potential, marine eutrophication, and biodiversity impacts, whereas hatchery stage dominated cumulative energy demand and water use. The nursery stage of laboratory rearing and the use of imported commercial feed emerged as major hotspots. Alternative scenarios based on renewable electricity and modified transport logistics reduced several impact categories, with local feed production providing potentially the most balanced improvements. Although restored oysters stored biogenic carbon, sequestration remained negligible compared with project emissions over a 10-year period. The study demonstrates that LCA is an effective decision-support tool for identifying environmental hotspots, optimizing restoration strategies, and integrating sustainability considerations into marine biodiversity restoration planning.

papers.title: Relevance of traditional knowledge of food preservation for disaster preparedness and climate change adaptation in Pacific Islands: A case study from Nabuna Village, Koro Island
papers.authors: Filipe Veisa, Viliamu Iese, Rosiana Lagi, Hilda Waqa-Sakiti
papers.abstract: Pacific Island communities face significant challenges from climate-related hazards, particularly tropical cyclones, which can disrupt food systems and undermine food security. Traditional Knowledge (TK) provides locally grounded knowledge of environmental conditions, seasonal patterns, food preservation and weather observation, but its transmission and use are changing alongside sociocultural and technological developments. This study examines traditional food preservation, seasonal knowledge and weather forecasting in Nabuna Village, Koro Island, Fiji, with particular attention to their use and transmission across generations. A qualitative case study was conducted, informed by resilience theory and socio-ecological systems (SES) thinking. Data were collected through six age-and gender-stratified focus group discussions with 30 participants aged 18–89 years and analyzed thematically to examine food preservation practices, seasonal indicators, weather forecasting and intergenerational knowledge transmission. Participants described pit storage of root crops, drying and smoking of fish, and seasonal preservation and use of breadfruit and yams in relation to the Fijian traditional calendar ( Vula Vakaviti ) and environmental indicators. Older participants described using ecological cues, including changes in cloud patterns, wind direction, bird behavior and food availability, when anticipating weather conditions and preparing food and water. Younger participants reported greater reliance on radio, television, mobile phones and social media for formal weather information, alongside varying familiarity with traditional indicators. The findings indicate the continued coexistence of traditional and formal sources of environmental information, while transmission and use of traditional knowledge vary across generations. The study highlights the context-specific relevance of traditional food preservation and environmental knowledge for understanding community responses to climatic and sociocultural change, while recognizing that the qualitative evidence does not independently establish causal effects on food security, adaptative capacity or disaster outcomes.

papers.title: Women’s political empowerment and climate change vulnerability in Sub-Saharan African (SSA): do institutional quality, culture, and religion matter?
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: This article examines the effect of women’s political empowerment on climate change vulnerability, from a sample of 39 sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries observed over the period 1995–2023, by mobilizing a fixed-effects country and time model estimated by the Two-Way Fixed Effect (TWFE). Two main results emerge: on the one hand, women’s political empowerment directly reduces climate vulnerability in SSA; on the other hand, political stability, democracy, and corruption control amplify this effect, while religion, ethnic, and linguistic fractionalization mitigate it. The robustness of the results is confirmed by the System Generalized Method of Moments (S-GMM), Two-Stage Least Squares with instrumental variables (IV-2SLS), Driscoll-Kraay, outlier exclusion, and placebo tests. The model remains sensitive to digital, environmental, and socioeconomic variables. These results suggest strengthening women’s political empowerment, consolidating formal institutions, adapting policies to cultural and religious contexts, and integrating socioeconomic and environmental dimensions into climate adaptation strategies.

papers.title: Veganism in the city: Capitalist assimilation or multispecies resistance?
papers.authors: Corey Lee Wrenn
papers.abstract: Cities are spaces in which consumerism, culture, and protest must often comingle. Often concentrated in urban spaces, veganism—which advocates alternative consumption, multispecies multiculturalism, and resistance to harmful foodways and unequal multispecies relationships—offers an interesting case study of urban consumerist dynamics. Using semiotic analysis of signs, posted menus, advertisements, and window displays collected between 2021 and 2022 in one university town in southeast England, it is considered how veganism might be able to persist, perhaps even thrive, in capital-serving cityscapes. Findings suggest that veganism is strained by the marketplace function of the city. Veganism is reduced to a form of consumption that aligns with capitalist interests, and anti-speciesist representations of veganism are lacking. Yet, this study also considers if the prevalence of vegan signage could be moderately subversive in normalizing veganism. These complexities are considered in the context of geographical and sociological research on cities as sites of both corporate co-optation of protest and social change.

papers.title: Provisioning otherwise: Platform co-operatives and the reworking of platform urbanism
papers.authors: J. Zhang
papers.abstract: Urban life is increasingly organised through platforms, but platform urbanism has largely been understood through corporate intermediation, extraction and regulation. This article asks what becomes visible when platformisation is approached instead through the politics of provision. Drawing on 31 semi-structured interviews across a translocal platform co-operative ecosystem, it examines how co-operatively governed digital infrastructures make shared provision workable across places. The article develops platformed mutual provisioning to describe a recursive process through which dispersed capacities are assembled around situated needs, extended through federation and kept collectively governable through maintenance, democratic learning and data stewardship. The findings show that platform co-operatives matter less as ownership alternatives in themselves than as fragile experiments in organising the coordinating capacities on which food systems, logistics and civic economies increasingly depend. Their significance lies in keeping those capacities revisable as they become infrastructural to everyday provision. The article argues that this opens a wider politics of co-operative infrastructural urbanism, in which digital urbanisation is judged not by growth or technological novelty, but by whether the power to coordinate provision remains answerable to those who depend upon it.

papers.title: Companions, not just services: What do experiences of time teach us about urban vegetation?
papers.authors: Soledad Martínez Rodríguez
papers.abstract: Urban nature literature often describes urban vegetation in terms of its ‘ecosystem services’ such as carbon sequestration, air filtering, noise reduction and soil permeability, among others. Studies also note that green spaces foster social cohesion by providing places for social encounters and activities. Nevertheless, the bodily and sensorial relationships that urban dwellers create with urban vegetation are overlooked within these accounts. From an anthropological view that understands places as human and other-than-human entanglements, urban dwellers’ relationships with vegetation are poorly captured by the more transactional concept of ‘ecosystem services’. In this commentary, I bring to light shared temporalities between urban walkers and vegetation to argue for a closer look at the intertwined complexities of human and more-than-human cohabitation. Based on ethnographic research in Osorno, a small city in southern Chile – often referred to as a ‘green city’ because of its abundant vegetation – I delve into the experiences and narratives that emerge from people’s everyday contact with urban vegetation through their everyday journeys on foot. They invite us to rethink what urban nature does to urban places and what it means for these walkers, which is more than just providing humans with some ‘services’. Here, I show how everyday encounters with urban vegetation invite people to experience time differently. People can attune to more-than-human temporalities through senses and affects, allowing them to recall past times and also be part of a cyclical time we – humans and other-than-humans – all share.

papers.title: Time as a commons: Collective temporal practices and the making of urban care infrastructures
papers.authors: Maro Pantazidou
papers.abstract: The contemporary care crisis has prompted a surge of scholarly attention to urban care commons and bottom-up care infrastructures, with particular emphasis on their socio-spatial dynamics. By contrast, the temporal dynamics through which such formations are sustained have received limited attention. While previous research has engaged urban and institutional temporalities in relation to processes of commoning, the commoning of time itself remains underexplored as a pathway towards urban transformation. This article turns to the urban co-production of time, focusing on the temporal patterns that sustain one of the largest self-organised collective kitchens in crisis-ridden central Athens. The kitchen mobilises dozens of residents in daily food provisioning and redistribution, preparing and sharing hundreds of warm meals 6 days a week. The scale and continuity of the initiative provide a unique empirical lens for understanding the organisational and meaning-making practices, at the temporal level, that make informal urban care infrastructures possible. Drawing on 10 months of ethnographic fieldwork, the article illuminates both the temporal resources (clock-time hours) and the temporal orientations (valuations of time beyond clock-time) that underpin alternative arrangements of social provisioning. The findings introduce the concept of collective time work to describe how otherwise temporally fragmented urban communities pool time and remake temporal norms to create cohesive community care. Conceptually, the article advances time as a relational, co-produced good, rather than an individually managed resource, to foreground the politics of time as a vital vector for transforming how care is organised and sustained in cities.

papers.title: Healthcare real estate and urban infrastructure: between public good and financial asset
papers.authors: Zhenyi Huang, Sotiris Tsolacos
papers.abstract: In contemporary urbanism, healthcare real estate plays the dual role of essential social infrastructure and financial asset. On the one hand, healthcare real estate functions as a vital form of social infrastructure, shaping patterns of accessibility, belonging, and resilience in cities. On the other hand, it is increasingly governed as a financial asset through public-private partnerships (PPPs), real estate investment trusts (REITs), and institutional investment. This article conceptualises healthcare real estate as a form of financialised social infrastructure situated at the intersection of public service provision, financial investment, and urban governance. Drawing on evidence from the UK healthcare estate, the article examines how healthcare real estate has become increasingly embedded within circuits of capital accumulation and integrated into broader processes of financialised urbanism. The analysis demonstrates that financialisation has reshaped the financing and governance of healthcare real estate, expanding the role of institutional investors and private capital and reinforcing investment logics within healthcare provision. While these developments can mobilise capital for infrastructure investment and estate modernisation, they may also generate governance challenges relating to ownership, accountability, accessibility, and spatial equity. The article contributes to urban studies by advancing understanding of healthcare real estate as a form of financialised social infrastructure and examining its implications for health equity and sustainable urban development. It further explores the potential of impact investment as a mechanism for reconciling financial and social objectives, highlighting the importance of impact evaluation frameworks in aligning private capital with broader social and spatial outcomes.

papers.abstract: This article examines urban food commons by tracing the emergence of food cultivation and preparation initiatives in urban peripheries, including occupied and contested territories. Drawing on feminist political ecology, decolonial feminist perspectives on urban commons and care and Black Food Geographies, our research reframes these environments not as deficient but as care infrastructures where commoning practices among plants, people and place are enacted. The research focuses on community gardens and solidarity kitchens in the Brazilian metropolitan region of Belo Horizonte, based on fieldwork and focus groups with members from a state–society network of food activists that have shaped the alternative food system in Belo Horizonte in the last three decades. Beyond the binary of ‘social fixes’ for capitalist urbanisation and localised prefigurative spaces of post-capitalist difference, we treat community gardens and kitchens as spaces for (re)organising social reproduction, reproducing a socio-natural network and providing care that can unlock transformative potentialities. Furthermore, we claim that these urban food commons sparked renewed state commitment, transforming not only the political ecology of food and the urban landscape in the peripheries of Belo Horizonte but also state policies, aiming at promoting state-commons. Tensions remain, however, considering the relationships between autonomy in commoning practices and the state. Our article contributes to discussions of urban food commons by examining their relational dynamics with the state.

papers.authors: Nicolette Duncan
papers.abstract: Melbourne city as it exists today is a colonial project with a history of destruction, exclusion and denial of local First Nations sovereignty on Wurundjeri Country. papers.title: Blind spots of state spatial selectivity: The left-behind secondary cities in Chinese mega-regionalisation
papers.authors: Yizhao Du, Rodrigo Viseu Cardoso, Roberto Rocco
papers.abstract: Chinese intra-regional unevenness remains unresolved, despite mega-regionalisation being promoted as the main instrument of state spatial selectivity aimed at alleviating polarisation and peripheralisation in secondary cities. We argue that a largely overlooked intermediate stage of such processes is partly responsible for the uneven outcomes of mega-regionalisation in tackling these challenges. This stage bridges mega-regional visions initiated by top-level authorities and practical interventions at the local scale, organised in action plans that determine relations between core and secondary cities by state actors at the provincial level. We select three representative Chinese mega-regions and examine the yearly reports from 2006 to 2024 of their provincial governments (acting as mega-regional coordinators) to summarise the various mechanisms and periodic trends of these plans through the analytical lens of historical institutionalism. We find that the intermediate stage, focused on spatial reconfiguration, redistribution of urban functions, and improving regional accessibility, emphasises cores as the driving force, leaving blind spots that allow only a few secondary cities to integrate and benefit from mega-regionalisation, whereas many more are further polarised and peripheralised. This is evidenced in all cases despite their different trends in specific action plans. We highlight the impact of intermediate-stage action plans on secondary cities to extend spatial selectivity theory to multi-scalar state-led regionalisation processes and call for policy and governance attention to intermediate-stage coordination mechanisms that allow representation of secondary cities in mega-regional planning.

papers.title: How fire mosaics influence landscape connectivity and genetic diversity of two Australian bat species
papers.authors: Amanda Lo Cascio, Robyn E. Shaw, Holly Sitters et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Context Dispersal is a fundamental ecological and evolutionary process, influencing population dynamics, and shaping biodiversity. Spatial and temporal variation in fire mosaics can influence gene flow and genetic diversity through effects on individual dispersal. Objectives We investigated the influence of fire mosaics on effective dispersal in two Australian microbat species with contrasting mobility, Chalinolobus morio and Vespadelus vulturnus , to predict species’ capacities to persist in changing environments. Methods In the heathy woodlands of south-east Australia, we used genomic, spatial and environmental data at multiple scales. We examined population level and within population fine-scale genetic structure, and landscape connectivity, which together serve as indirect proxies for effective dispersal (dispersal followed by successful reproduction). These analyses allowed us to assess how fire mosaics influence dispersal pathways and identify potential barriers or sex-biases to dispersal. Results Both species showed limited population subdivision. Vespadelus vulturnus exhibited isolation by distance and fine-scale genetic structure consistent with dispersal limitation, whereas C. morio showed only weak fine-scale structure and no isolation by distance. Spatial genetic patterns were consistent with each species’ scale-dependent responses to the fire mosaic: in C. morio genetic distance decreased with the amount of late-successional habitat at the 3 km scale (a weak signal consistent with enhanced gene flow), whereas in V. vulturnus genetic distance decreased with fire-age diversity and edge density, and increased with late-successional habitat. Genetic diversity showed no significant response to fire mosaics in either species, although weak negative associations with the amount of long-unburnt vegetation in V. vulturnus at broader scales (5–6 km) may indicate that habitat features limiting movement erode diversity over longer timeframes. Conclusions Fire-mediated differences in habitat suitability can influence gene flow, shaping genetic structure and landscape connectivity. Microbat genetic structure is consistent with the species’ traits and ecological requirements, thereby linking post fire habitat succession to genetic response in fire-prone landscapes.

papers.title: Interpretable machine learning for seasonal nitrate and total phosphorus concentrations integrating hydrologic, land-use, and ecological indicators
papers.authors: Gbenga Daniels, Meghna Rajbhandari, Amanda Carneiro Marques
papers.abstract: Diffuse nutrient pollution remains difficult to assess because nutrient concentrations reflect interacting watershed, hydrochemical, ecological, and hydrologic conditions that vary across space and time. Although machine-learning models incorporate multiple environmental predictors, the contribution of different predictor domains can be difficult to distinguish when all variables are evaluated simultaneously. This study developed an interpretable machine-learning framework to predict seasonal nitrate and total phosphorus concentrations across seven watersheds in southeastern Pennsylvania using observations from 2002 to 2024. Physicochemical, land-cover, ecological, climatic, and hydrologic information were progressively integrated through four predictor scenarios, allowing the added predictive value of each domain to be evaluated. Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models were independently optimized for each scenario. Predictive performance improved as broader environmental information was incorporated, with the largest gain occurring after land-cover variables were added to the physicochemical baseline. The environmental-only M4 XGBoost models achieved test R 2 values of 0.858 for nitrate and 0.770 for total phosphorus, with RMSE values of 0.624 and 0.170 mg L −1 , respectively. Repeated site-stratified validation of the nitrate M4 model yielded a mean test R 2 of 0.834 ± 0.026, indicating stable performance across alternative partitions. SHapley Additive exPlanations identified forest cover, developed land cover, and specific conductance as dominant predictors for both nutrients, while discharge contributed more strongly to nitrate and dissolved oxygen to total phosphorus prediction. These reveal that land-cover composition offers significant prognostic insights beyond in-stream conditions, whereas hydrochemical and hydrologic factors aid in differentiating nutrient-specific trends. The framework could guide the prioritizing of watershed monitoring and the evaluation of nutrient dynamics.

papers.title: The accelerating northward expansion of the South Asian High has slowed regional sea ice melt in the Arctic
papers.authors: Bingyi Wu, Siqin Xie, Yuqing Sha et al.
papers.abstract: Summer Arctic sea ice affects Arctic shipping, the regional ecological environment, atmospheric blocking highs, and even the subsequent East Asian winter monsoon variability; consequently, the mechanisms governing its evolution have received extensive attention. This study investigates impacts of the South Asian High (SAH) on the slowdown of Arctic regional sea ice melt through diagnostic analyses and nudging experiments. Results show that the northward expansion of the SAH has strengthened Arctic tropospheric westerlies and intensified the polar vortex over the Arctic Ocean and the Pacific sector of the Arctic. These changes have slowed summer sea ice melt in the Pacific sector of the Arctic by reducing surface net shortwave radiation and enhancing anomalous sea ice drift into the region. More importantly, the coupling between the northward expansion of the SAH and the changing Arctic has systematically strengthened since the early 2000s. This northward expansion acts as the key driver in the dynamical linkage between the intensified Arctic tropospheric westerlies and the occurrence of extreme heatwaves in the region from the Yangtze River basin to the south of Japan. On decadal timescales, this study reveals an identical turning point of both the northward expansion of the SAH and the Arctic summer 500-1000 hPa thickness pattern, which corresponds well to the onset of accelerated oceanic warming in the North Pacific. Simulation experients show that global sea surface temperatures has driven the accelerating northward expansion of the SAH, rather than Arctic sea ice melt. The findings of this study suggest that the northward expansion of the subtropical systems has profound implications for the changing Arctic ecosystem.

papers.authors: Katherine A. Culbertson, Sarah Federman, Lucia Catherine Camp, Matthew D. Potts
papers.abstract: Given the existing gap in biodiversity funding, mobilizing private finance will be essential to achieving global biodiversity conservation goals, especially across lower- and middle-income countries with limited capacity and public finance. The emerging voluntary biodiversity market (VBM) holds promise to leverage private finance for biodiversity, but credit-generating protocols must be robust to prevent greenwashing and maximize effectiveness. In this study, the first to move beyond theoretical critiques and general market assessments of the VBM, we extracted details of program structure and crediting issuance from protocols for 13 relatively well-established biodiversity-crediting organizations. With these data, we evaluated protocols’ alignment with both conservation and restoration biology principles and lessons learned from the voluntary carbon market (VCM). We find that action must be taken to improve quantification of biodiversity impacts, especially incorporating patch size and connectivity in crediting and assessing projects on ecologically relevant timelines. Further, safeguards for additionality, leakage, risk, and verification from the VCM must be more robustly integrated in the VBM, and deep engagement and investment in local communities must be improved to ensure durable biodiversity-positive outcomes.

papers.abstract: Abstract The South China Sea (SCS) is one of the most active marginal seas for tropical cyclones (TCs) worldwide and a key region for TC hazards along the coasts of southern China, Philippines and Vietnam. Here, we show that the number of TCs reaching Category 3-5 intensity has increased significantly, with more occurring in the northern SCS. This change is primarily linked to an increasing contribution of western North Pacific TCs entering through the Luzon Strait, which experience weaker land-induced weakening than those crossing the Philippine archipelago and retain greater intensity for subsequent development. papers.abstract: Abstract Increases in high‐elevation wildfires in California’s Sierra Nevada region (SNR) have raised concerns about potential impacts on snowpack, a major source for the state’s water supply. Quantifying fire-induced changes in snow storage remains challenging in mountainous regions with complex topography and large climatic and ecological gradients, due to limited field observations and process models. This study leveraged high-resolution Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) lidar surveys (2023-2024) to assess the impacts of 2020-2021 wildfires on peak snow water equivalent (SWE) across six SNR watersheds. We assembled >32,000 matched burned-unburned 50-m pixel pairs with similar pre-fire environmental conditions and assessed how changes in peak SWE (ΔpeakSWE: burned - unburned) varied with burn severity, pre-fire forest structure, meteorological variables, and terrain above the snowline. Across matched pairs, post-fire peak SWE differences varied in both magnitude and direction, depending on yearly weather (e.g., wet vs. normal year) and local environmental setting. The largest positive burned–unburned difference occurred in dense forests with ≥75% canopy loss at intermediate elevations in 2023, where burned areas had 13.0 cm higher peak SWE on average (12% relative to the matched unburned mean of 105.1 cm); this difference was substantially smaller in 2024. The spatially cross-validated extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model showed terrain provided the strongest predictive information, followed by vegetation structure. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and a shallow decision tree further showed that sites with lower heat exposure, locally lower terrain positions, and intermediate elevations generally were associated with higher peak SWE in burned areas compared to matched unburned areas, whereas taller pre-fire canopies and exposed, high-energy terrain were associated with lower peak SWE. These results demonstrate wildfire effects on peak SWE are strongly context dependent and provide an assessment framework for anticipating where high elevation wildfires may increase or reduce mountain snow storage.

papers.authors: Zejiang Yin, Zhang Lei, Song Yang et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Subtropical East Asia, among the world's most densely populated regions and a major agricultural region, has experienced pronounced early-spring drying since the 1980s, posing growing risks to water resources and agriculture. However, the relative contributions of external forcing and internal variability to the drying trend, as well as the associated dynamic and thermodynamic processes, remain unclear. The circulation analogues-based dynamic adjustment reveals that atmospheric circulation changes explain approximately 108% of the observed drying trend, which were largely driven by internal variability. These circulation changes are closely linked to a positive-to-negative phase transition of the Interdecadal Pacific Variability (IPV), which can suppress precipitation by weakening the Northwest Pacific anticyclone and inducing anomalous subsidence over subtropical East Asia. papers.title: Mitigating downstream thermal stress and hydropeaking through reservoir operation in Alpine systems
papers.authors: Maria Elena Alfano, Davide Poggi, Laura Savoldi, Marta Zaniolo
papers.abstract: Multi-objective reservoir optimization plays a key role in managing water scarcity and growing uncertainty in hydrological inputs in sensitive mountain environments. While existing computational frameworks for multi-objective operation are effective in balancing traditional competing uses such as hydropower production and water supply, they often provide a simplified representation of environmental impacts. In particular, operationally driven alterations of flow regimes (hydropeaking) and downstream water quality, especially water temperature, are rarely incorporated as explicit objectives, despite representing some of the most critical stressors on Alpine riverine ecosystems. In this work, we advance the representation of environmental impacts in reservoir operation frameworks by coupling a classic hourly mass balance with a physically based energy balance, which explicitly resolves reservoir-induced water temperature alterations. We design reservoir operating policies that seek to minimize thermal stress and hydropeaking, and maximize hydropower revenue and irrigation reliability through Evolutionary Multi-Objective Direct Policy Search. Applied to the Ceresole reservoir in Gran Paradiso National Park (Italy), the framework generates a Pareto front that balances the four objectives. The revenue cost of reducing hydropeaking and thermal stress grows steeply as the two objectives approach their minima, while in the rest of the front the three non-economic objectives are loosely coupled and can be improved together. The most effective strategies mitigate thermal stress by advancing winter drawdown and managing summer storage levels to buffer the seasonal stratification cycle, achieving a substantial reduction in thermal alteration at a modest cost to hydropower revenue. Relative to the historical operation, policies with revenue within 1% of the baseline value reduce irrigation deficit, thermal stress and hydropeaking by up to 63%, 32% and 33%. Ecosystem-aware operation can therefore reduce several stressors while preserving economic value, an approach that can be tested in other Alpine systems under climate pressure.

papers.title: China’s carbon neutrality strengthens its photovoltaic potential: Co-benefits for climate action and energy security
papers.authors: Lei Jin, Yixiong Lu, Jianping Tang et al.
papers.abstract: Solar photovoltaic (PV) power is central to China’s carbon neutrality strategy, but the extent to which mitigation reshapes the climate resource base for PV generation remains uncertain. Here we combine Earth system simulations with a 0.1°-resolution deep learning downscaling framework to quantify changes in China’s meteorological PV potential under divergent emission pathways. We find that the carbon-neutral SSP2-com pathway not only stabilizes but actively strengthens national meteorological PV potential by century’s end (+0.27% relative to 1981−2010 baseline), whereas high emissions trigger a persistent decline (−0.49%). Crucially, stringent mitigation induces a fundamental spatial restructuring: it shields premium solar resources in western China from severe depletion (e.g. Tibet: −0.42% under SSP2-com versus −1.23% under SSP3-7.0), while substantially boosting meteorological PV potential in historically resource-constrained eastern provinces (e.g. Guizhou: +1.05%, Hunan: +1.04%, Jiangxi: +0.97%, Fujian: +1.07%). This asymmetric response reduces interprovincial disparities in solar resource availability. Factor-separation analyses attribute most changes to shortwave radiation rather than temperature or wind speed, consistent with aerosol-related brightening under stringent mitigation. Our findings reveal that carbon neutrality functions not merely as a climate corrective but as a potential driver of energy security, potentially contributing to a solar landscape with greater spatial equity and resilience.

papers.title: Diagnostic analysis of the prolonged 2022 South Asia heatwave
papers.authors: Narayana Reddy Karrevula, Binisia Sanatan, Diana Francis et al.
papers.abstract: The 2022 South Asian heatwave was among the most extreme events recorded in the past half-century, with temperature anomalies exceeding 6°C in several regions. However, the large-scale processes governing its evolution, persistence, and spatial expansion remain insufficiently understood. Using reanalysis, satellite, and observational datasets, this study investigates the synoptic- and planetary-scale conditions associated with two distinct phases: 11–30 March and 31 March–20 April 2022. Phase-I was characterized by enhanced quasi-geostrophic stationary wave activity, a persistent heat dome over South Asia, and vertically coherent warm anomalies extending through much of the troposphere. Phase-II featured the spatial expansion of the heatwave from Southwest Asia toward Central and South Asia, coinciding with a transition of the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) from its positive to negative phase. The contrasting phases also exhibited distinct surface energy-budget characteristics, with Phase-I associated with enhanced radiative forcing and Phase-II characterized by stronger sensible heating, enhanced downward longwave and net radiation, and comparatively weak latent heat flux, consistent with reduced evaporative cooling. The broader-domain analysis further indicates that the Phase-II response extended beyond the core heatwave region. These findings highlight the potential role of NAO-related circulation variability in the regional evolution of the heatwave and demonstrate that its contrasting phases were associated with different combinations of large-scale atmospheric dynamics and land–atmosphere interactions.

papers.abstract: In late July 2023, North China experienced a devastating extreme precipitation event, resulting in severe flooding and massive economic losses. While extreme circulation patterns, abundant moisture transport, and local topography have been identified as the key drivers, the specific role of anthropogenic warming remains elusive. By comparing hindcast simulations of the actual event with a counterfactual scenario representing a climate without anthropogenic interference, we calculate that human-induced warming increased total precipitation by 7.6% and amplified the risk for extreme precipitation at the 400 mm threshold by 9.6%. Additionally, warming facilitated the development of more organized convective systems, characterized by fewer but larger convective clusters, alongside increased precipitation intensity and spatial extent. Our findings reveal the roles of moisture transport and convective structure associated with anthropogenic warming during this extreme rainfall event, highlighting the escalating threats posed by such extremes to communities, infrastructure, and economies.

papers.abstract: Pavement crack analysis is a representative benchmark problem for intelligent visual inspection, requiring detection of thin, low-contrast, topologically irregular structures under severe class imbalance. papers.authors: Xin Liu, Rui Zheng
papers.abstract: Time‐based rates are widely used in risk communication, yet little is known about how their framing shapes perception and behavior. This article distinguishes between two common frames of rate—the average‐time frame (e.g., “one death every 30 seconds”) and the average‐outcome frame (e.g., “two deaths every minute”). Four studies were conducted to examine the rate framing effects on perceived risk and behavioral intention. A pilot text analysis of Weibo posts showed that the average‐time frame was relatively more prevalent in COVID‐19 risk communication and generated higher user engagement. Across three studies ( N = 979), we found that the average‐time frame elicited higher perceived risk than the average‐outcome frame, and such a rate framing effect weakened as the objective risk level increased. Moreover, framing information in an average‐time format effectively promoted intentions to limit sedentary behavior. These findings identify a new framing effect in risk communication and offer practical implications for designing persuasive public health messages.

papers.authors: Ekky Amiral Faqi, Ragil Andika Yuniawan, Samuel Jonson Sutanto
papers.abstract: Landslides are one of the most devastating hazards globally, including in Indonesia. To reduce casualties, Indonesia has established the Blueprint of Indonesian Landslide Early Warning System (BILEWS). This system currently relies on rainfall-induced landslide thresholds for issuing the warning signals derived from historical landslide occurrences in Java, Sumatra, and Kalimantan Islands. However, landslide occurrence is strongly influenced not only by rainfall but also by antecedent soil moisture conditions and soil characteristics. Therefore, BILEWS still faces technical challenges in accurately predicting landslides, especially in Sulawesi and Papua Islands, where Java’s threshold is applied there. This study aims to enhance the existing rainfall thresholds and incorporate soil moisture into a multi-variable threshold framework. Specifically, rainfall thresholds, soil moisture thresholds, and the combination of rainfall-soil moisture thresholds are developed. In addition, the relationship between soil moisture and landslide occurrence is evaluated across different soil textures. The results indicate that the optimal thresholds vary across islands. The existing rainfall thresholds yield the highest performance in Java and the Sumatra Islands with Youden Index of 0.545 and 0.740, respectively. In Sulawesi Island, the best performed threshold is the newly developed rainfall threshold with a Youden Index of 0.477. The rainfall-soil moisture thresholds show optimum performance for Kalimantan (0.465) and Papua (0.458) Islands. Furthermore, soil moisture significantly affects landslide risks in sandy clay loam and loam soil textures. Developing thresholds based on significant soil textures improves the performance of landslide prediction.

papers.authors: Jiahao Wang, Norberto C. Nadal-Caraballo, Yi Zhao et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract To reduce the impact of tropical cyclones (TCs) under uncertain future climate projections, developing TC hazard curves across a range of potential climate scenarios is essential for risk-informed resilience planning in coastal regions. Probabilistic TC hazard analyses typically rely on synthetic TC datasets, generated by full-track TC models that include genesis, track, and intensity/decay components. However, simulating the entire TC life cycle can accumulate biases from genesis and intensification stages, requires extensive environmental inputs and computational resources, and may inadequately represent landfall characteristics. To reduce these limitations, this study applies the synthetic TC datasets obtained from the ImpeRIal College Storm (IRIS) model. IRIS focuses exclusively on the post-lifetime maximum intensity (LMI) evolution. In addition, many prior studies primarily rely on two-dimensional (2D) slab TC wind field models or simpler models to expedite hazard analyses. This further reduces the reliability of the hazard analyses since 2D slab models integrate vertically across the boundary layer and treat the flow as height-invariant. This study leverages newly developed synthetic TC datasets and a height-resolving three-dimensional (3D) TC wind field model that accounts for intercity land-cover differences, and applies the peak over threshold–generalized Pareto distribution (POT-GPD) statistical model to generate TC hazard curves for various future climate scenarios at the state and city levels; and then assesses the changes in TC frequency and intensity under these scenarios. The results suggest an overall intensification of TCs and an increase in the total number of landfalling TCs, especially stronger TCs, under warmer climate scenarios.

papers.title: Flood risk assessment frameworks under climate change: a review
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: Flood risk assessment (FRA) has become increasingly important under climate change, yet its conceptual and methodological foundations remain heterogeneous. This paper presents a systematic literature review, structured according to the ROSES reporting standards, that synthesises foundational, policy, general, sector-specific and site-specific approaches to FRA, with particular attention to the EU Floods Directive (2007/60/EC) and to highly influential flood-risk literature. Rather than judging specialised frameworks against a single universal model, the review distinguishes transferable methodological elements from context-dependent design choices. FRA is generally organised around combinations of hazard, likelihood, exposure, vulnerability, consequences and capacity, but these components are defined and operationalised differently across scales, sectors and decision contexts. Site-specific GIS and multi-criteria studies provide locally useful workflows whose indicators and weights require recalibration elsewhere, while infrastructure frameworks appropriately incorporate sector-specific data such as inspections, network criticality and operational thresholds. Methodological diversity is therefore partly necessary and becomes problematic mainly when definitions, assumptions and aggregation rules are not reported transparently. The synthesis links flood mechanisms to their analytical emphasis, users and decision purposes; outlines practical options for treating non-stationarity, including non-stationary frequency models, climate-model ensembles, joint-probability methods, stress testing and periodic updating; and proposes five design principles for future FRA. The review concludes that the appropriate goal is structured comparability, that is, transparent reporting of the flood mechanism, decision purpose, likelihood method, vulnerability construction, uncertainty and transferability conditions, rather than methodological homogenisation.

The decision tree correctly classified fan presence or absence in 80% of the 235 drainage basins analyzed, including 76% of the 145 extension basins. Overestimation of debris-flow fans occurred in several basins; however, field surveys confirmed the presence of debris-flow deposits from the 2003 event, indicating that the decision tree could successfully identify hazardous basins even where fans have been eroded or artificially modified. Morphological indicators in most basins where debris-flow fans and occurrences were overlooked were close to the threshold for fan formation, demonstrating that decision tree analysis enables the effective identification of error sources, which is a clear advantage over more complex machine learning methods. Furthermore, the topographic data required for debris-flow fan detection are more readily available than historical records of debris-flow occurrences. Therefore, decision tree analysis based on debris-flow fan distribution offers a practical, interpretable, and widely applicable tool for identifying drainage basins with high debris-flow potential.

papers.title: A multi-variable threshold approach to landslide prediction: integrating rainfall, soil moisture, and soil texture in Indonesia
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: Landslides are one of the most devastating hazards globally, including in Indonesia. To reduce casualties, Indonesia has established the Blueprint of Indonesian Landslide Early Warning System (BILEWS). This system currently relies on rainfall-induced landslide thresholds for issuing the warning signals derived from historical landslide occurrences in Java, Sumatra, and Kalimantan Islands. However, landslide occurrence is strongly influenced not only by rainfall but also by antecedent soil moisture conditions and soil characteristics. Therefore, BILEWS still faces technical challenges in accurately predicting landslides, especially in Sulawesi and Papua Islands, where Java’s threshold is applied there. This study aims to enhance the existing rainfall thresholds and incorporate soil moisture into a multi-variable threshold framework. Specifically, rainfall thresholds, soil moisture thresholds, and the combination of rainfall-soil moisture thresholds are developed. In addition, the relationship between soil moisture and landslide occurrence is evaluated across different soil textures. The results indicate that the optimal thresholds vary across islands. The existing rainfall thresholds yield the highest performance in Java and the Sumatra Islands with Youden Index of 0.545 and 0.740, respectively. In Sulawesi Island, the best performed threshold is the newly developed rainfall threshold with a Youden Index of 0.477. The rainfall-soil moisture thresholds show optimum performance for Kalimantan (0.465) and Papua (0.458) Islands. Furthermore, soil moisture significantly affects landslide risks in sandy clay loam and loam soil textures. Developing thresholds based on significant soil textures improves the performance of landslide prediction since no single threshold fits all.

papers.title: Projection of tropical cyclone wind-speed hazard curves under future climate scenarios for coastal design and resilience planning
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: To reduce the impact of tropical cyclones (TCs) under uncertain future climate projections, developing TC hazard curves across a range of potential climate scenarios is essential for risk-informed resilience planning in coastal regions. Probabilistic TC hazard analyses typically rely on synthetic TC datasets, generated by full-track TC models that include genesis, track, and intensity/decay components. However, simulating the entire TC life cycle can accumulate biases from genesis and intensification stages, requires extensive environmental inputs and computational resources, and may inadequately represent landfall characteristics. To reduce these limitations, this study applies the synthetic TC datasets obtained from the ImpeRIal College Storm (IRIS) model. IRIS focuses exclusively on the post-lifetime maximum intensity (LMI) evolution. In addition, many prior studies primarily rely on two-dimensional (2D) slab TC wind field models or simpler models to expedite hazard analyses. This further reduces the reliability of the hazard analyses since 2D slab models integrate vertically across the boundary layer and treat the flow as height-invariant. This study leverages newly developed synthetic TC datasets and a height-resolving three-dimensional (3D) TC wind field model that accounts for intercity land-cover differences, and applies the peak over threshold–generalized Pareto distribution (POT-GPD) statistical model to generate TC hazard curves for various future climate scenarios at the state and city levels; and then assesses the changes in TC frequency and intensity under these scenarios. The results suggest an overall intensification of TCs and an increase in the total number of landfalling TCs, especially stronger TCs, under warmer climate scenarios.

papers.title: Detection of a meteotsunami in the Colombian Caribbean and its role as a driver of coastal morphodynamics
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: On July 19, 2017, a high frequency sea-level fluctuation was observed in Santa Marta, Colombia, causing local coastal inundation. Local authorities attributed these tsunami-like waves to a submarine landslide, through no scientific study confirming this interpretation has been published. In this paper, we present an alternative hypothesis: that the tsunami-like waves were triggered by the passing of a squall line, which resulted in rapid, localised pressure disturbances, triggering sea surface level oscillations that were amplified to a meteotsunami via resonance effects in the shallow coastal waters of an abandoned delta lobe of the Magdalena River. We present GOES satellite observations and ERA-5 Reanalysis data to characterize the squall line and test whether resonance could have taken place. The persistence of strong wind and intense up- and downdrafts even in the hourly averaged ERA-5 data, the coincidence of the arrival of the system in shallow water with the detection of the tsunami-like waves in tide gauges, and the detected travel-speed of the system that supports resonance development lend support to the hypothesis. To our knowledge, no previous meteotsunamis have been reported in the Colombian Caribbean. To assess the geomorphic impact of such an event, this study analyzes wave-run-up and total water levels (TWL) associated with the event, finding that they are comparable to those observed during moderate storms in the area. We further show that the event drove significant geomorphic change by inducing breaching of a lagoon.

papers.title: Global Flood Mapper v2: open-access flood mapping and exposure assessment with Sentinel-1 SAR
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: We present Global Flood Mapper v2 (GFM v2), which adds flood depth estimation, on-demand GeoTIFF export, cloud-based impact assessment against high-resolution land cover and five global population datasets to quantify exposure uncertainty, and parameter-encoded URLs for reproducibility and sharing. Its predecessor, GFM v1, was already an open-access, globally operational web portal for rapid, analysis-ready flood mapping that runs entirely in the browser without coding, downloads, or data preprocessing; GFM v2 builds on this foundation without sacrificing that ease of use. Unlike fully-automatic monitoring services, which publish precomputed output from fixed, provider-set detection parameters and do not process every Sentinel-1 acquisition, GFM v2 gives users direct control over which acquisitions are processed and how: users can compare pre- and during-flood imagery, adjust detection thresholds and terrain masks to local conditions, and select any area and date, so that small-scale or localized events can be mapped more flexibly, whether or not an automated monitoring service has covered them. By providing these capabilities in the browser without sacrificing user control, GFM v2 supports timely, evidence-based flood response and management.

papers.title: Mind the gap: Quantifying vegetation-gap frequency and length along least-cost routes among urban green spaces
papers.authors: Matthew J. Lundquist
papers.abstract: Urban green infrastructure planning for enhancing biodiversity can benefit from information about the connectivity between large green spaces and existing small, vegetated patches embedded within cities. While the importance of habitat connectivity for biodiversity is well established, the size and frequency of vegetation gaps between green spaces may influence functional connectivity within cities. LiDAR-derived vegetation height data were used to map potential vegetated corridors linking publicly managed green spaces in New York City, USA. Least-cost path models identified routes that preferentially followed high (>5 m), medium (1–5 m), and low (0.3–1 m) vegetation while excluding buildings and assigning higher costs to gaps in the selected vegetation class. Across 77,116 park pairs, routes were completed for 98.4–99.1 % of pairs, depending on vegetation class, but their gap patterns differed significantly. Mean (± SE) gap counts were 12.1 ± 0.3, 17.5 ± 0.3, and 25.6 ± 0.4 per route in high, medium, and low vegetation, respectively. Mean within-route gap lengths ranged from 11.9 ± 0.3 m (medium vegetation) to 15.1 ± 0.3 m (high vegetation), and 5.6–8.1 % of routes contained gaps exceeding 100 m. Short gaps accumulated, however: total gap length exceeded 100 m on 56–77 % of routes. These results suggest that existing urban vegetation forms potential corridors among public green spaces, but with extensive gaps in individual vegetation classes. By locating larger gaps and areas with limited vegetated access, this type of modeling can help direct habitat assessment and greening toward opportunities to improve ecological connectivity.

papers.title: Biodiversity and ecosystem services in changing landscapes: a biome level scenario assessment for continental Ecuador
papers.authors: Hongmi Koo, Janina Kleemann, Pablo Cuenca et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Context Ecuador hosts remarkable biogeographical areas, including the Coast, the Andes and the Amazon, which represent distinctive biomes. However, a comprehensive assessment accounting for biome-specific differences in the landscape as well as in biodiversity and ecosystem services (BES) across Ecuador is still lacking. Objectives This study tested an integrative approach that combines spatial modeling and participatory methods for the impact assessment of future scenarios (deforestation and afforestation) on BES. Important ecosystem services included food, drinking water, service water, soil erosion control, water flow regulation, pollination, macro climate regulation, and landscape aesthetic/amenity. Methods The BES were identified by experts through surveys and workshops. Additionally, the experts were involved in developing simulation conditions for the scenarios, which were applied in the spatially explicit modeling platform based on Geographic Information System and Cellular Automaton modules. Results The scenario impacts were visualized as changes in landscape configuration and BES capacities at the biome level. Regarding the deforestation scenarios, the Amazon biome showed the most notable change, with 11–13% of loss in most BES except food provision. However, the BES of the Andean biome presented the most evident trade-offs between BES by the afforestation scenarios with an approximately 10% decrease in food provision, while there was a 20–30% increase in other BES. BES capacity maps for all three biomes clearly showed that BES hotspots were reduced by the deforestation scenarios, whereas the afforestation scenarios expanded BES hotspots. Conclusions Experts’ feedback on the applied methods and the results confirmed the usefulness of the BES assessment for future landscape management with further consideration of how to transfer the findings into policy-related information.

papers.title: Drivers of biodiversity in mineral extraction sites – a cross-taxa analysis with implications for management and restoration
papers.authors: Katharina Schwesig, Vera Marie Alida Zizka, Christoph Scherber, Norbert Hölzel
papers.abstract: Extraction sites are often considered sources of environmental damage. However, in intensively used and nutrient-enriched landscapes they may also provide exceptional secondary habitats, shaped by disturbance and nutrient depletion. Their contribution to biodiversity across taxonomic groups remains insufficiently understood, and integrated guidelines for managing biodiversity during active extraction are needed. We examined terrestrial and aquatic biodiversity across twelve active German extraction sites of limestone, gypsum, sand and gravel. Data on vascular plants, soil parameters and six insect groups were collected via vegetation relevés, soil samples, DNA metabarcoding from trap samples and transect walks on 103 terrestrial plots. Aquatic diversity (Amphibia and Odonata) was assessed at 75 water bodies using transect walks and eDNA metabarcoding. Across all sites, we recorded 2054 species, including 168 threatened in Germany. Species composition varied strongly across substrate types and between plots. Terrestrial insect diversity increased with plant species richness, while higher latitude, which was correlated with sampling year, and the proportion of shrubs had negative effects. The respective insect groups showed group-specific responses to plot age, the proportions of open soil, active extraction area and surrounding grassland. To maximise conservation value, particularly for terrestrial insects, site management should promote habitat heterogeneity and allow the formation of temporary habitats through natural succession. Increasing vascular plant richness boosts local insect diversity. Embedding biodiversity management into the regional context can create networks of valuable secondary habitats. Extraction sites thus bear a high but so far underused potential to advance restoration targets beyond existing protected areas.

papers.title: Decomposing drivers of global temperature change after net zero
papers.authors: Annika Högner, Zebedee Nicholls, Gaurav Ganti
papers.abstract: Abstract Net-zero CO2 (NZCO2) and greenhouse gas emission (GHG) targets are central to the development of mitigation scenarios. Projected global surface air temperature (GSAT) change after NZCO2 depends on several factors that broadly fall into two categories: scenario-specific factors that account for the diversity of possible mitigation pathways to net zero and beyond, and model-specific factors that describe the climate system response, captured in the zero emissions commitment (ZEC). Current established climate assessment approaches do not separate contributions from these two categories to post-net-zero GSAT change in GHG emission scenarios. To address this shortcoming, we propose a diagnostic protocol that decomposes the contributions from the model-specific ZEC and from key scenario-characteristics including non-CO2 GHG reductions, net-negative CO2 emissions, and other climate forcers. We assess the GSAT outcomes from a large collection of scenarios that achieve NZCO2 using the MAGICC model. We find a peak warming increase of 0.08°C (‘likely (>66%)’ 0.05 to 0.11°C) per decade delay in reaching NZCO2 and a -0.11°C (likely -0.13 to -0.05°C) post-NZCO2 GSAT decline by 2100. Based on our decomposition approach we find that the model-specific negative ZEC contributes about -0.03°C across the full scenario set. This is on the same order as the contribution from non-CO2 mitigation for scenarios that achieve NZGHG. The decomposition allows us to test the sensitivity of our outcomes. We apply the IPCC AR6 WGI assessed value of 0°C (likely ±0.19°C) for ZEC and find that the median likelihood of no further warming on multidecadal timescales after achieving and maintaining NZCO2 drops from just about 85% to 67%. After achieving and maintaining NZGHG, however, it remains ‘very likely (>90%)’. This underlines the need for setting preventive mitigation targets to account for potential stronger than expected Earth system feedbacks and demonstrates the utility of a decomposition approach.

papers.title: Significant albedo-induced cooling effects across tropical and subtropical dryland biomes
papers.authors: Hongze Pei, Jieming Chou, Chaoyang Wang et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Terrestrial ecosystems can significantly regulate climate through carbon uptake and alterations in surface albedo. However, current climate mitigation assessments largely focus on carbon sinks while overlooking albedo-induced radiative effects. We developed an integrated framework to quantify the net climate effect of global terrestrial ecosystems from 2001 to 2019 by combining net ecosystem productivity with albedo-induced radiative forcing. We estimated the Net Equivalent Carbon Dioxide Stock Change (NESC), which incorporates both Net Cumulative Carbon uptake Equivalent (NCCE) and the Emission Equivalent of Shortwave Forcing (EESF). Results show that global terrestrial ecosystems generated a net cooling effect of 397.52 Gt CO2e during the study period. Among biomes, tropical and subtropical grasslands, savannas and shrublands, and deserts and xeric shrublands, contributed a cooling effect of 95.33 Gt CO2e due to increased albedo, nearly one-quarter of the total NCCE across the 14 biomes, largely driven by declines in photosynthetic vegetation and soil drying in Land use and land cover (LULC) non-conversion areas. These findings provide new perspectives for re-evaluating the climate value of terrestrial ecosystems and a scientific basis for incorporating surface albedo into future nature-based solutions for climate mitigation.

papers.title: Viewing extreme precipitation intensification through an absolute-change lens
papers.authors: Jiayi Ni, Changrui Zhu, Qun Yue et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract While relative fractional changes are widely used to characterize extreme precipitation intensification under climate warming, absolute changes provide a complementary perspective that more directly quantifies the magnitude of extreme precipitation intensification, with direct implications for assessing potential impacts. By analyzing annual maximum daily precipitation in climate models, we show that the geographical patterns of the strongest extreme precipitation intensification identified from absolute changes differ from those highlighted by relative changes, and that the most intense annual maxima exhibit substantially larger absolute increases than weaker annual maxima despite only modest differences in their relative changes. Although thermodynamic moistening produces broadly similar relative increases in stronger and weaker annual maxima, it leads to substantially larger absolute increases in stronger maxima, primarily owing to differences in climatological intensity. Dynamic contributions reinforce this intensity-dependent contrast in some regions, particularly in the South and East Asian monsoon regions and equatorial Africa. These contrasts highlight the value of considering absolute changes alongside relative changes to better characterize the magnitude and geographical patterns of extreme precipitation intensification and inform assessments of potential impacts under climate warming.

papers.authors: Chiara Colesanti Senni, Justin A. Johnson
papers.abstract: Abstract Global assessments of climate, biodiversity, and ecosystem services rely on projections of land-use change (LUC), typically from integrated assessment models (IAMs) at coarse resolution (25 to 50 km) and downscaled to the 30 to 300 m required by biophysical models. The choice of LUC projection introduces large variation in results, but this variation is rarely assessed. For Brazil, we systematically compare two LUC projections, a regionally calibrated model (Land Use and Cover Change Modelling Environment, LuccME) and a global product (Land-Use Harmonization 2, LUH2), downscaling both to 300 m with the Spatial Economic Allocation Landscape Simulator (SEALS) and computing five sustainability indicators (biomass carbon, biodiversity intactness, water yield, Forest Code compliance, and a diffuse-nitrogen index). The differences are large, from −37 to +45 % for biomass carbon, −20 to +23 % for water yield, −76 to +12 % for the diffuse-nitrogen index, and −0.27 to +0.17 in mean species abundance. The choice between the two projections also flips the Forest Code compliance call on 9 to 26 % of Brazil's land grid cells, and several biome-level shifts reverse sign under an alternative class correspondence, a sensitivity we quantify. Differences of this size could materially affect sustainability analyses, including REDD+ accounting, where a shifted carbon baseline could change results-based payments, as well as biodiversity assessment and nature-related financial-risk analysis.

papers.title: Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States
papers.authors: Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving substantial growth in electricity demand from data centers in the US, yet how the resulting air quality and public health impacts are distributed remain poorly quantified. To trace the ambient air pollution and associated premature mortality impacts of grid-supplied data center electricity demand in 2023, we couple the United States Electricity Generation Optimization model with the GEOS-Chem chemical transport model. We compare hourly, unit-level electricity dispatch with and without data center demand to quantify changes in power-sector emissions, ambient PM and ozone, and associated premature mortality. Our results show that electricity generation attributable to data center demand is largely supplied by fossil fuel units across multiple regions, resulting in additional annual mean PM concentrations of 0.02–0.08 g m (local peak concentrations up to 0.2 g m ), and regionally varying ozone responses characterized by wintertime depletion and summertime enhancement. These impacts are most pronounced in the Midwest United States, where marginal emissions from coal-fired units and ammonia-rich atmospheric conditions enhance secondary particulate formation. We estimate that this grid-supplied demand is responsible for 513 (95% CI: 469–557) annual premature mortalities from PM and an additional 137 (95% CI: 90–183) annually from maximum daily 8 h average ozone (MDA8- ) in the contiguous US. State-level analysis reveals a systematic geographic mismatch: states hosting the largest data center loads do not necessarily experience the highest attributable mortality rates, while some states with little data center demand bear substantial burdens. This mismatch arises because of dispatch across interconnected electricity regions, regional differences in generation and emissions, and atmospheric chemistry and transport, which together separate the locations of demand from those of exposure and mortality. These findings highlight the importance of considering both air quality impacts and their spatial distribution in data center and macro-energy system planning.

papers.title: Communicating heat risk: the psychological impact of naming and ranking heatwaves on threat perception & protective behavior
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: Extreme heat has emerged as the most lethal weather-related threat globally, yet warning systems often fail to motivate protective behavior, creating a critical gap in climate adaptation policy. Guided by the Extended Parallel Process Model, this study experimentally tests whether two communication cues borrowed from other hazard domains, personalized naming and categorical ranking, enhance public threat perception and protective intentions. A 2 × 2 randomized survey experiment ( N = 1,047) was conducted with a U.S. online sample, manipulating the presence of each cue in a standardized heatwave warning. Single-item Likert scales administered immediately after exposure measured the model’s three threat appraisal components (Perceived Severity, Perceived Vulnerability, and Fear) and Protective Behavioral Intentions. Linear regression models assessed main and moderation effects, controlling for demographic and climate belief covariates. Categorical ranking significantly increased all three components of threat appraisal. Naming had no measurable effect. Combining both cues was less effective than categorical ranking alone, suggesting a cognitive interference effect that may undermine complex messaging. The analyses also identified heterogeneity in how threat appraisal translates into protective intentions: men responded more strongly to fear and women to perceived vulnerability, while political affiliation moderated responses to perceived severity. These findings suggest that cognitive simplicity, not personalized naming, makes heat warnings more effective at raising perceived threat. They offer preliminary guidance for designing heat warning systems, pending replication across populations and real-world settings.

papers.title: Assessing just access to urban ecosystem services through spatial multi-criteria decision modeling: Evidence from a Global South city, Dhaka
papers.authors: Md. Nazmul Haque, Ayyoob Sharifi
papers.abstract: Recent urban development in Dhaka has created injustices in access to Urban Ecosystem Services (UES), affecting resilience, health, and well-being. This study evaluates the status of justice in access to UES through spatial modeling. Four UES were analyzed: recreation and tourism (cultural), urban cooling (regulating), habitat quality (supporting), and water yield (provisioning), using the InVEST model. Accessibility within a 15-minute walk from ward centroids was assessed with the Enhanced Two-Step Floating Catchment Area method. In addition, a multidimensional environmental justice framework was operationalized to examine justice scenarios in Dhaka, using the Best–Worst Method. Finally, a composite Justice in Access to UES (JAU) Index was constructed by integrating UES supply, accessibility, and justice indicators through a fuzzy overlay operation. The findings highlight significant injustices in access to UES across Dhaka. The highest proportions of very low JAU values were observed for Cultural (51%) and Supporting (47%) UES. A clear divide emerged, with Dhaka South consistently lagging behind Dhaka North across all services. Dhaka North Ward 19 (Hatirjheel area) and Dhaka South Ward 03 (near Hatirjheel) recorded the highest JAU values across all UES types, yet large portions of the city remained underserved. Overall, the results demonstrate that justice in access to UES depends not only on supply or accessibility, but also on the interplay of spatial configuration, social vulnerability, and structural barriers. Addressing these injustices requires equity-focused urban planning to strengthen services in marginalized neighborhoods and promote inclusive, sustainable urban development in Dhaka.
